strengths: The paper provides a clean theoretical result (Theorem 3.1) showing exact equivalence between layer-wise local-SSL updates and global BP-SSL gradients in deep linear networks under orthonormality, with a correct and transparent proof (including a batched version in Appendix A). This gives a principled explanation for why local-SSL underperforms global BP-SSL in practice.

The theory is genuinely used to drive algorithm design: the analysis of broken orthonormality (Theorem 3.3) motivates direct top-down feedback (CLAPP++DFB), and the analysis of BP gradients in convnets motivates spatially dependent projections B^l. This theory-to-practice pipeline, with cosine-similarity measurements of gradient updates (Figures 2-4, A2), is a convincing methodology.

Strong empirical validation on CIFAR-10, STL-10, and Tiny ImageNet with 4-seed confidence intervals: CLAPP++ variants substantially outperform prior local-SSL methods (SCFF, LPL, Stochastic FF, original CLAPP) and reach parity with matched BP-SSL baselines (BP-CLAPP++ and BP-InfoNCE) on the same VGG architecture.
A unifying formalism (Table 1) that encompasses CLAPP, Forward-forward, PhyLL, and SCFF is a useful conceptual contribution and clarifies the relationships among local-SSL rules.

Thorough treatment of baselines and controls: naive DFA and predictive-coding attempts on the SSL objective (Appendix C, Table A3), rank-constrained B^l ablations (Figure A1), a theoretical 'optimal local-SSL' upper bound on BP approximation (Definition 3.4), and gradient alignment measured at multiple training stages.

The paper is honest about scope: the authors explicitly state the theorem does not carry over to nonlinear networks, that FF-style normalization could not be handled, and that the BP-InfoNCE baseline is not the global SSL state of the art. Hyperparameters and architectures are documented sufficiently for reproduction.
weaknesses: The assumptions behind Theorem 3.1 are strong and not satisfied in practice: deep linearity, exactly orthonormal (square, constant-width) weight matrices at the moment of update, and a strict timescale separation in which B^l instantaneously reaches its optimum. The theory is therefore largely inspirational for the practical algorithm, and the paper does not quantify how much of the practical gain is attributable to the theory versus heuristic design choices.

Theorem 3.3, which motivates direct feedback, holds only for linear f, whereas the actual CLAPP loss uses f(x)=max(0,1-x); the non-linear case is only supported numerically. This weakens the tightness of the theory-practice link for the main algorithmic contribution.

The state-of-the-art claim against SCFF compares numbers from the literature, potentially across different architectures, augmentations, and training budgets; a same-architecture reimplementation or additional standardized comparison would strengthen this claim. The SOTA claim is also confined to a small regime (VGG-scale convnets, moderate accuracy: ~81% CIFAR-10, ~38% Tiny ImageNet), and no larger-scale or modern architecture (ResNet) experiments are provided.

The spatially dependent B^l introduces many projection matrices (per-location blocks), raising memory and biological-plausibility concerns; the sharing scheme (Table A2) partially mitigates this, but an explicit analysis of memory/compute cost relative to CLAPP and BP is deferred to future work.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a paper whose central claims rest on custom gradient-alignment experiments and re-implementations of several baselines.

The result that gradient-alignment correlates with downstream performance replicates a known finding from the supervised local-learning literature (which the authors acknowledge); the novelty of this part lies mainly in transplanting the philosophy to SSL rather than in a new principle.

The equivalence in deep linear networks with orthonormal weights relies on a fairly standard cancellation argument; the significance of Theorem 3.1 is more conceptual than technically deep, and the practical relevance of exact equivalence under conditions never met in real training is limited.

strengths: The paper provides a clear unifying formalism (Table 1) that casts CLAPP, Forward-Forward, PhyLL, and SCFF into a common layerwise loss structure, which is conceptually useful for comparing local-SSL rules.

Theorem 3.1 (exact equivalence of local-SSL and BP-SSL updates in deep linear networks with orthonormal weights) is a clean result, and the authors honestly enumerate its restrictive assumptions (orthonormality, learnable and unconstrained B^l, timescale separation) and verify numerically which conditions matter (Figure 2).

The theory is actually used to derive algorithmic changes (2D spatially dependent projections B^l, direct feedback from the last layer), and ablations (Figure 5, Table 2) attribute the largest performance gain to the theory-motivated spatial dependence, which supports the theory-to-practice narrative.

The empirical evaluation includes confidence intervals over seeds, ablations (with/without spatial dependence, DFB, both), and negative results for naive DFA and predictive coding adaptations of SSL losses (Appendix C, Tables A3-A4), which strengthens the baseline picture.
The result that CLAPP++ variants approach BP-SSL performance on CIFAR-10/STL-10/Tiny-ImageNet and surpass SCFF is a genuine advance for the local-SSL subfield.
weaknesses: The central theory-practice link is weaker than claimed. In realistic settings (ReLU MLP, Figure 3B; convnets, Figure 4C), cosine similarity of local-SSL gradients to BP gradients in early layers remains low (~0.2-0.4), yet the paper opens Section 4 by asserting local-SSL is 'almost the ideal approximation of BP-SSL update.' If performance matches BP despite large early-layer misalignment, gradient alignment is not clearly the explanatory variable, undermining the causal story the paper is built on.

The exact equivalence theorem applies only to deep linear networks; the authors themselves concede it 'does not carry over to nonlinear networks' and could not be extended even to normalized linear networks (as needed for Forward-Forward). The headline claim ('Can local learning match self-supervised backpropagation?') is therefore answered affirmatively only under conditions far from the setting where the performance results are obtained.

The theoretical results rely on strong idealizations: instantaneous optimization of B^l to B^l_* (timescale separation), orthonormal weights, and for Theorem 3.3 only a linear f with batch size one. The proofs also contain loosely argued steps (e.g., the norm argument in the Theorem 3.1 proof) that would benefit from a fully rigorous treatment.

Part of the performance improvement is confounded with changes not motivated by theory: the baseline itself adds SimCLR augmentations and multi-layer concatenated readout relative to original CLAPP (73.29 -> 74.51 on STL-10 from readout alone). The SOTA comparison against SCFF and other methods should control for these non-theoretic modifications more carefully.

Scale and generality are limited: all experiments use a single VGG-style architecture on CIFAR-10/STL-10/Tiny-ImageNet with a linear probe. The paper acknowledges the BP-InfoNCE baseline is not the state of the art of global BP-SSL, so 'matches the performance of comparable global BP-SSL' is a relatively modest bar by modern SSL standards.

The biological plausibility discussion (apical dendrites, top-layer feedback, cortical connectivity) is speculative and not tested; the claimed memory advantage of CLAPP++DFB is deferred to future work rather than quantified.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and several experimental details (e.g., how spatially dependent B^l patches are chosen, hyperparameters for the 300-epoch training) are spread across the appendix without a clear statement that code will be made available.

strengths: Well-motivated goal: building a theoretical bridge between local self-supervised learning rules (CLAPP, Forward-forward, SCFF, LPL) and global BP-SSL, an area where theory has been missing.

Theorem 3.1 gives a clean exact-equivalence result for deep linear networks with orthonormal weights, and the authors honestly state its restrictions (equal widths, linear networks, trainability of B^l reaching optimum instantaneously).

Good theory-to-practice loop: the theory directly motivates two concrete algorithmic changes (direct feedback from the last layer; spatially dependent 2D projections B^l), each of which is verified both in gradient-alignment simulations and in downstream accuracy, including ablations that remove assumptions one at a time (Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4).

Empirical results are meaningful for this subfield: CLAPP++ variants surpass SCFF (previous local-SSL SOTA) on CIFAR-10, STL-10, and Tiny ImageNet, and reach parity with the same-architecture BP-SSL baselines (Table 2), with 95% CIs over 4 seeds.

The appendix honestly explores alternative BP-approximation methods (DFA, predictive coding) and reports negative results, plus a definition of an 'optimal local-SSL' upper bound showing the gap to ideal BP approximation is nearly closed.

The unified formalism (Table 1) encompassing multiple local-SSL rules is a useful conceptual contribution, and biological interpretation (Eq. 6, apical dendrite gating) is thoughtfully connected without overclaiming.
weaknesses: The exact equivalence holds only under restrictive conditions (linear networks, orthonormal weights, equal layer widths, batch size 1, B^l optimally adapted instantaneously). The authors acknowledge these, but the practical algorithms operate far outside these conditions, where gradient alignment in early layers is only ~0.2-0.4 (Figures 2-4), leaving a substantial unexplained gap between 'poor gradient alignment' and 'matched performance'.

The headline claim that local-SSL 'matches' global BP-SSL rests on a relatively weak BP baseline: a VGG with a linear projection head and last-layer SSL loss. The authors admit BP-InfoNCE is 'not the state-of-the-art of global BP-SSL'; stronger architectures (ResNet, non-linear heads) are known to do much better, so the significance of reaching parity is diluted.

Potential confound in the spatial-dependence result: making B^l spatially dependent increases its effective capacity/expressivity, so the performance gain may stem from added model capacity rather than improved BP approximation. The paper argues via gradient-alignment correlations but does not fully disentangle these factors.

Some empirical margins are small relative to reported error bars: e.g., CLAPP++both 81.18 ± 0.18 vs BP-CLAPP++ 80.49 ± 0.20 on CIFAR-10, and CLAPP++ 80.51 vs SCFF 80.60; claims of 'best performance across all datasets' are on the edge of statistical significance in places.

Theorem 3.3 (direct feedback improves alignment) requires f to be linear; the extension to softplus/realistic settings is only empirical, and the proof (Appendix A.2) involves several technical steps that would benefit from closer verification.

Resource efficiency claims (memory footprint reduction of CLAPP++DFB) are deferred to future work and not quantified, despite being listed as a motivation; no code release is explicitly stated, which limits reproducibility of the 300-epoch VGG experiments.

The local vs. global framing could be more carefully positioned relative to prior greedy layerwise SSL work (e.g., Lowe et al. 2019) — the core novelty (top-down reference vector and spatially structured B^l) is somewhat incremental even if well executed.

strengths: Clear theory-to-practice pipeline: Theorem 3.1 identifies exact conditions (orthonormal weights, optimal trainable projections) under which layer-wise local-SSL updates equal global BP-SSL gradients in deep linear networks, and the subsequent algorithmic changes (direct feedback, 2D spatial dependence) are directly motivated by analyzing which conditions fail.

Theoretical claims are verified numerically with careful ablations (removing orthonormality, linearity, learnability of B^l one at a time; Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure A1), which strengthens confidence in the theory and in the diagnosis of where local-SSL diverges from BP.

The proposed CLAPP++ variants set a new state of the art for local-SSL on CIFAR-10, STL-10, TinyImageNet and ImageNet, and match the comparable BP-SSL baselines (BP-CLAPP++, BP-InfoNCE) on CIFAR-10, STL-10 and TinyImageNet, with confidence intervals from 4 seeds.

Thorough comparison against alternative BP-approximation frameworks (DFA, predictive coding, naive CLAPP variants) in Appendix D, showing that simply applying existing BP-approximation machinery to SSL losses fails — this substantiates the claim that the contribution is non-trivial.
Good reproducibility: code is stated to be available, architectures, pooling sizes, optimizers, learning rates and hardware are specified in detail (Tables A1-A5, Appendix C).

The paper is honest about limitations: the theory does not carry over to non-linear networks, the architectures are VGG-based rather than ResNets, and the ImageNet gap versus BP remains; the biological-plausibility discussion is measured and connects DFB to known cortical feedback phenomenology.
weaknesses: The exact-equivalence theory (Theorem 3.1) rests on strong and somewhat unrealistic assumptions: orthonormal weight matrices 'at the moment of gradient update' (which will not hold during actual training), batch size one in the main proof, convex f, instantaneously optimal B^l on a separated timescale, and linear activations. The title's question is only answered exactly in this idealized regime; for the non-linear convnet experiments the connection is qualitative (cosine similarity), not a guarantee.

The central empirical claim 'local-SSL reaches the performance of BP-SSL' depends on relatively weak BP baselines: BP-CLAPP++ and BP-InfoNCE use linear projection heads and a VGG architecture, and the paper acknowledges the BP-InfoNCE baseline is not state-of-the-art global SSL. On ImageNet the gap is still substantial (44.16 vs 55.19), so the headline claim should be read as dataset- and architecture-specific.

The 2D spatial dependence makes B^l's parameter count grow linearly with image size, and the claimed VRAM/throughput benefits (Table 3) are estimates; the experiments use a mathematically equivalent stop-gradient implementation (Algorithm 3) rather than the ideal memory-free local algorithm, so the efficiency claim is not fully validated end-to-end.

Theorem 3.3 (direct feedback helps under shrinking widths) is proven only for linear f, and its generality to the actual losses used (softplus, hinge) is supported empirically rather than theoretically; the practical benefit of DFB over CLAPP++ alone is small on some datasets (e.g., ImageNet: 44.16 vs 42.55, with CLAPP++both slightly lower than CLAPP++DFB there).

Biological plausibility, a stated motivation, is somewhat weakened by the introduced mechanisms: structured spatially dependent feedback matrices and learning signals from the top layer are argued to map onto cortical connectivity, but this remains speculative and is not a prediction-tested claim.

Only one architectural family (VGG-style convnets) is tested for the empirical claims; the extent to which the gradient-alignment diagnosis predicts performance gains in modern architectures (ResNets, transformers, residual connections) is left as future work.

strengths: The paper provides a clear theoretical framework (unified notation for CLAPP, Forward-forward, PhyLL, SCFF) and proves exact gradient equivalence between local-SSL and global BP-SSL in deep linear networks under explicit conditions (orthonormal weights, constant width, trainable/optimized B_l, no normalization). The assumptions are stated honestly, and the authors verify each condition by removing them one at a time (Figure 2), which is good scientific practice.

The theory is genuinely used to guide algorithm design: the direct feedback (DFB) modification (Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.2) and the 2D spatial dependence (Proposition 3.5) both follow from the analysis, and each is validated both by gradient-alignment measurements and downstream classification gains. This theory-to-practice pipeline is more rigorous than typical empirical local-learning papers.

Empirically, CLAPP++ variants set a new state of the art among local-SSL methods on CIFAR-10, STL-10, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet, with 4-seed confidence intervals for their own results, and they include useful negative controls (DFA and predictive coding fail badly on SSL objectives, Appendix D).

The evaluation includes a well-motivated theoretical 'optimal local-SSL' upper bound (Definition 3.4) showing their method is close to the best achievable local approximation of BP, which strengthens the claim that remaining discrepancies are inherent rather than sloppiness.

The paper discusses limitations candidly (ResNet/residual connections unaddressed, ImageNet gap persists, BP-InfoNCE baseline is not SOTA global SSL), and the VRAM/wall-clock analysis quantifies a practical benefit of local learning.
No ethical concerns; the impact statement is appropriate for this type of work.
weaknesses: The core theory applies only under restrictive conditions (deep linear networks, orthonormal weights, constant width, batch-size-one for some results, instantaneous optimization of B_l) that are violated in every practically relevant experiment. The paper acknowledges this, but the link between Theorem 3.1 and the performance gains of CLAPP++ in non-linear convnets is ultimately correlational: better gradient alignment and better accuracy co-occur, but no evidence is given that alignment is causal, nor is a theory provided for the non-linear case.

The 'local-SSL matches BP-SSL' headline claim depends on a weak BP baseline. BP-CLAPP++ and BP-InfoNCE use a VGG architecture with linear projection heads, far from modern global SSL (SimCLR/BYOL/VICReg with ResNets). Matching this baseline on CIFAR-10/STL-10/TinyImageNet while a ~4-10 point gap remains on ImageNet makes the title-level claim ('Can local learning match...?') only partially supported.

A significant practical limitation is hidden in the implementation: the ideal local-SSL algorithms (Algorithms 1-2, which would realize the VRAM savings and true locality) were not used for the reported benchmarks; instead a mathematically equivalent stop-gradient implementation (Algorithm 3) was used. The claimed 38-60% VRAM savings are therefore estimates, not demonstrated end-to-end results.

Some claims of biological plausibility (apical dendrites, neuromodulators, structured cortical connectivity) in Section 5 are speculative and stretch well beyond what the 2D spatial dependence and DFB mechanisms establish; the spatial-dependence parameterization via adaptive pooling kernels is an engineering choice rather than a biological prediction.

Reproducibility concerns: the code URL in the paper is incomplete ('Code is available at' with no link on page 1), which should be fixed. Additionally, several baseline numbers are reproduced 'from our own simulations' without detail on how closely they match published values, and key hyperparameters (e.g., pooling kernel sizes per layer in Table A2) appear somewhat dataset-tuned without an ablation of sensitivity to these choices.

The novelty is moderate: block-wise/local SSL with InfoNCE-type losses (Greedy InfoMax, Siddiqui et al. 2024) and spatially structured feedback already exist; the contribution is a careful theory plus incremental, well-motivated modifications, which is valuable but not a fundamental advance.

strengths: The paper establishes a genuine theoretical bridge between local self-supervised learning rules (CLAPP, Forward-forward, SCFF, PhyLL) and global BP-SSL: Theorem 3.1 gives exact gradient equivalence in deep linear networks under clearly stated conditions (orthonormal weights, trainable Bl reaching optimum, no normalization), and Corollary 3.2 extends this to direct feedback. This is a novel unifying result for the local-SSL literature.

The theoretical insights are productively translated into algorithmic changes: 2D spatial dependence in the projection Bl (justified by Proposition 3.5 for linear convnets) and direct feedback from the last layer (Theorem 3.3). Both are verified numerically via gradient cosine-similarity measurements (Figures 2-4), and the theoretical optimum Δ° (Definition 3.4) provides a meaningful upper-bound analysis showing the proposed method is close to the best achievable local approximation.

Comprehensive empirical validation across CIFAR-10, STL-10, TinyImageNet and ImageNet with 95% confidence intervals over 4 seeds. CLAPP++ variants set a new state of the art for local-SSL (Table 2) and match BP-CLAPP++ and BP-InfoNCE baselines on three of four datasets. The ablation (CLAPP++ without spatial dependence at 73.21% vs. 80.51% on CIFAR-10) cleanly attributes the gains to the theory-guided change rather than to incidental modifications such as SimCLR augmentations.

Valuable additional evidence: naive DFA and predictive coding baselines for SSL objectives (Appendix D, Tables A4/A5) establish that existing BP-approximation frameworks do not trivially solve this problem; VRAM/wall-clock analysis (Table 3) quantifies a practical advantage of locality; rank-constrained B (Figure A1) and training-stage analyses (Figure A2) probe the theory further.

Limitations are honestly discussed: the theory does not extend to nonlinear networks or to normalized FF variants; ImageNet remains below BP-SSL; the BP-InfoNCE baseline is not SOTA global SSL (VGG + linear projection head); and the bridge to ResNets is flagged as future work. The Δ° construction is correctly identified as non-local and used only for analysis.

Reproducibility is good: code is available, architectures and hyperparameters are specified in detail (Appendix C, Tables A1-A5), and the unified formalism (Table 1) makes the framework understandable across algorithms.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between the idealized theory (deep linear networks, orthonormal weights, instantaneously optimal Bl, batch-size-one proofs) and the practical setting. The theorem conditions cannot be verified during actual convnet training, so the causal link between 'improved gradient alignment' and 'improved accuracy' rests on correlation across ablations rather than a tight theoretical guarantee for non-linear networks. Theorem 3.3 additionally requires a linear f and is only extended to softplus empirically.

The headline claim 'matches the performance of global BP-SSL' is carefully scoped but could be over-read: it holds against comparable VGG/linear-projection-head baselines on CIFAR-10, STL-10, and TinyImageNet, and does not hold on ImageNet (42.49 vs. 55.19 for BP-InfoNCE). The practical significance of the result is therefore bounded to modest architectures; the paper acknowledges this, but readers should not conclude locality is closed in general.

The presentation is dense in places: notation involving z, c, B, superscripts pos/neg and the two loss types takes effort to parse, and some proof sketches in the main text (e.g., the orthonormality-based norm argument) require careful reading; more intuitive explanation of why spatial dependence matters could aid accessibility.

Some comparisons inherit choices from prior work (training setup of Illing et al. 2021, 300 epochs) without exploring whether CLAPP++ variants are sensitive to these; the claim of SOTA is restricted to algorithms the authors could find in the literature, which is reasonable but necessarily incomplete.

The biological interpretation (Section 5) is suggestive rather than validated; claims linking CLAPP++DFB to apical dendritic integration and spatial dependence to cortical connectivity are speculative, though appropriately framed as interpretation.

The practical VRAM advantage was estimated analytically rather than demonstrated with a full training run of the ideal algorithms (Algorithm 1/2), with the experiments instead using a mathematically equivalent stop-gradient implementation (Algorithm 3).
